title: Theoretical prediction for monitoring Jahn-Teller vibrational evolution using real-space tip-enhanced Raman imaging

paper_content.abstract: The Jahn-Teller effect (JTE) reduces the geometrical symmetry of a system with degenerate electronic states via vibronic coupling, playing a pivotal role in molecular and condensed systems. However, due to the intrinsic limitations of conventional techniques, only the electronic evolution in JTE can be measured. Herein, we theoretically propose that vibrational resolved tip-enhanced Raman scattering images can visualize the vibrational evolutions in JTE in real space. Taking an experimentally accessible single zinc phthalocyanine (ZnPc) molecule as a proof-of-principle example, not only the degenerate vibrational splitting but also the overlooked vibration mixing caused by the JTE in its anionic form can be characterized by Raman images. Leveraging Raman images, the controllable configuration of JTE distortion with partial isotopic substitution can be further identified. These findings establish a practical protocol to monitor the detailed vibrational evolutions when a single molecule experiences JTE, providing a pathway for visualization of spontaneous symmetry breaking in molecular and solid-state systems.
paper_content.introduction:
The Jahn-Teller effect (JTE)1,2 describes a fundamental phenomenon that a degenerate system spontaneously reduces its geometry symmetry via the vibronic coupling to stabilize the total energy3–5. JTE represents a general mechanism of spontaneous symmetry breaking, which is responsible for various important observations across multiple disciplines, including spectroscopy, molecular and solid-state physics, stereochemistry, and materials science6–14. In practice, JTE can be efficiently induced by injecting or removing an electron from a degenerate electronic state15,16, particularly in systems containing transition metal ions7,17,18. Such a charge-induced JTE arises from the modification of electronic occupancy, which directly lifts the degeneracy of molecular orbitals and thereby triggers symmetry-lowering structural distortions. In this context, scanning probe microscopy (SPM) techniques provide a practical means to precisely control JTE in real space19,20.

Despite the success of SPM techniques in the visualization of JTE, most investigations were focused on imaging the symmetry breaking of electronic states21–25. Exclusive investigation on the electronic degrees of freedom in JTE has led to the current lack of understanding of its vibrational aspect, which results in potentially ambiguous assignments of accompanying frequency splitting, the mixing of vibrational wavefunctions upon symmetry reduction, and the possibility of controlling JTE distortions through atomic displacements. Recently, by leveraging the tip-enhanced Raman scatting (TERS)26–29, an experimental measurement has captured several spectral variations when a single zinc phthalocyanine (ZnPc) was negatively charged30, where vibrational frequency evolution was highlighted. Nevertheless, it still lacks further reports on imaging vibrational symmetry breaking, another essential aspect of JTE, although it is possible owing to the high spatial resolution of TERS31–35.

Recent TERS studies have demonstrated their ability to quantitatively map the spatial distribution of vibrational wavefunctions32,36–39. In this study, this technique is expected to be further extended to visualize the single-molecule JTE from the vibrational perspective. Taking the experimentally accessible ZnPc molecule as a proof-of-principle example, we theoretically propose that TERS images provide a practical means to monitor all the details of the vibrational evolution in JTE distortion. We demonstrate that, not only the splitting of degenerate vibrations but also the mixing of non-degenerate vibrations belonging to different irreducible representations of the high-symmetry point group, can be affirmatively observed in TERS images. For the latter case, we reveal that the mixing strength is determined by both the energy difference and spatial distribution overlap between the mixed modes. Moreover, we manifest that the controllable JTE distortions at the sub-ångström level achieved through partial isotope substitution can be unambiguously distinguished by high-resolution TERS imaging.
paper_content.results:
Spectra characterization of charge-induced JTE
Figure 1a illustrates the experimental setup for injecting an electron into neutral ZnPc to induce JTE distortion. In the neutral state, ZnPc possesses a doubly degenerate lowest unoccupied molecular orbital. Upon adding an extra electron, this degeneracy is lifted, triggering a symmetry-lowering structural distortion. Previous experiments observed sudden changes in TERS spectra when the sample bias exceeded 0.3 V, which was assigned as a transition from the neutral to negatively charged state30. It should be stressed that owing to the insulating spacer layer introduced in Fig. 1a, the negatively charged ZnPc− has a sufficiently long lifetime for spectral measurements and even imaging30,40. Besides, the experiment explicitly ruled out molecular deformation induced by mechanical pressure from the tip apex. Specifically, the reproducible spectral evolution during tip approach and retraction confirmed that the observed spectral changes and symmetry reduction originated intrinsically from different charging states of ZnPc30. Calculations show that the JTE-induced geometrical distortion from the neutral D4h to the anionic D2h is quite subtle (the elongations along both the diagonal axes are 0.026 and 0.010 Å, respectively, as shown in Fig. 1b), which provides an ideal example for focusing exclusively on vibrational variation itself.

To efficiently excite the required highly localized plasmonic field for single-molecule TERS measurements, an incident light with a wavelength of 532 nm was employed in the experiments30. Under the same incident energy, our first-principles calculations accurately reproduce the corresponding observed Raman spectra of ZnPc powder30 except for few peaks with relative intensities below ≈5% of the strongest band (e.g., a peak around 800 cm−1, Fig. 1c). Theoretical analysis reveal that these peaks originate from Raman-inactive modes because of the symmetry breaking via molecular stacking and lattice interactions in ZnPc powder. This undesired symmetry breaking is absent for a single molecule. Thus, the experimentally adopted wavelength of 532 nm can be used without further calibration in the practical calculations for single-molecular TERS. Then, we adopt an effective field Hamiltonian approach (see “Methods” for details), in which the spatial amplitude distribution of the localized plasmonic field is incorporated as the quantized light-matter interaction operator33,41–44, to enable the quantitative simulation of bond-resolved TERS spectra. By placing a 3 Å spatially confined plasmon (SCP) at the same tip position in the experiments, i.e., above the joint position between the lobe and center of ZnPc (see the black cross in Fig. 1b), the calculated TERS spectra for both neutral ZnPc and anionic ZnPc− are in overall agreement with their experimental counterparts (Fig. 1d). Specifically, the two main bands in the calculated spectrum of ZnPc− are located at 1309 and 1512 cm−1, which are in good agreement with the experimental values of 1305 and 1518 cm−1. For neutral ZnPc, one main peak in the theoretical spectrum appears at 1348 cm−1, which is again in agreement with the experimentally measured band at 1340 cm−1. As a result, the calculated TERS spectrum of ZnPc− presents a 39 cm−1 redshift caused by JTE, which quantitatively agrees with the corresponding experimental observation of 35 cm−1.30 For another main band, although the frequency shifts are in qualitative agreement, the theoretically predicted blueshift (26 cm−1) is larger than that (7 cm−1) measured in the experiments30. This result arises from the sole frequency deviation of the peak for neutral ZnPc, i.e., the band around 1511 cm−1 observed in experiments, as shown in Fig. 1d. Further calculated and experimental Raman images (see “Methods” for details) for this band are in excellent agreement with each other (Supplementary Fig. 1), demonstrating the affirmative assignment of this main band. In addition, the JTE-induced shifts of other secondary bands in the calculated spectra also agree well with the experimentally observed redshifts (Supplementary Fig. 2). The reproduction of the measured references in both uniform and plasmonic fields validates the accurate descriptions of electronic and vibrational structures as well as their responses at the current theoretical level.

According to the calculations, the experimentally measured30 two dominant bands for ZnPc and ZnPc− (Fig. 1d) are assigned to different vibrational modes. Specifically, the degenerate ν108 and ν105 contribute to the dominant bands of ZnPc. In ZnPc−, these vibrations split as a consequence of JTE and are labeled with subscripts “a” and “b” hereafter. As a result, the dominant high-frequency band originates from the accidentally degenerate ν0103a and ν025, where the superscript “0” denotes the anionic form. Meanwhile, ν048 contributes to the dominant band with low frequency, with the shoulder assigned as ν0108b. Although this assignment is different from ref. 30, the observation of only a single splitting component, i.e., ν0108b in ZnPc−, indicates the spatial localization of degenerate vibrational modes during symmetry breaking induced by JTE.

Imaging the degenerate vibrational splitting
To directly visualize the localization, we turn to vibrationally resolved TERS imaging36–38,45,46. By moving tip positions and simultaneously collecting scattering intensities at a given Raman shift, the images of the two dominant bands of ZnPc under an experimentally feasible 3 Å SCP (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4)37 were calculated as shown in Fig. 2a. Both images exhibit clear fourfold symmetrical patterns, which correspond to the Eu irreducible representation in D4h point group (see vibrational displacements in Fig. 2a). On the other hand, the dominant modes of ZnPc− give two-fold symmetric patterns (Fig. 2a), demonstrating the symmetry reduction from D4h to D2h owing to JTE. The individual contributions of component modes to images in Fig. 2a can be found in Supplementary Figs. 5–7. It should be stressed that, although bias voltages and a decoupled substrate were used to stabilized different charge states of ZnPc30, these effects on the vibrational modes and Raman images are negligible (Supplementary Figs. 8–10). This result is consistent with the general purpose of introducing the decouple layer in TERS experiments30 and should be attributed to the rigid backbone and flat adsorption configuration of ZnPc. For other systems with strong substrate-adsorbate interactions, adequately large cluster models with advanced charge localization calculations would be required for the accurate description of the substrate effects.

Detailed analysis reveal that at the central Zn position, the image of ν048 is constructive, which is opposite to the destructive feature in that of ν108. This result further confirms that the dominant bands observed in experiments30 originate from different vibrational modes. To determine the split modes of degenerate vibrations, for example, ν108 that involves vibrations at four interior nitrogen atoms, we focused a 3 Å SCP on the nitrogen atoms along different axes in ZnPc− (see the color-marked crosses in the inset of Fig. 2b). The calculated spectra manifest that when the SCP is located at one specific position, one split mode becomes active and another one is completely suppressed (Fig. 2b), which arises from the vibrational localization accompanying with the splitting of degenerate modes. These spectral outcomes of JTE under plasmonic fields are quite different from those under conventional uniform optical fields, where both split Raman bands can be simultaneously observed in the latter. As a result, the split modes (ν0108a and ν0108b) can be identified. Specifically, TERS images of these vibrations exhibit split patterns derived from the original ν108, with a destructive center, as anticipated (Fig. 2c).

With the correct assignment, the electronic and displacement redistribution effects can be unambiguously investigated for the splitting of degenerate vibrations when the molecule experiences a JTE distortion. Particularly, adding an extra electron to neutral D4h ZnPc would split the degenerate ν108 at 1348.0 cm−1 into a blue-shifted mode at 1352.5 cm−1 and a significantly red-shifted mode at 1319.6 cm−1. The Eu ν108 mode then becomes further localized, which results in two non-degenerate modes, i.e., a B2u mode (ν0108a) at 1345.6 cm−1 and a B3u mode (ν0108b) at 1323.5 cm−1 (Fig. 2c). The decomposition of electronic and vibrational effects is a general approach. The detailed analysis for other representative degenerate modes can be found in Supplementary Fig. 11. It should be stressed that the minor geometrical distortion caused by JTE in ZnPc enables the decomposition of these effects.

Imaging the non-degenerate vibrational mixing
The minor geometrical distortion also allows explicit visualization of another vibrational evolution, i.e., the mixing of non-degenerate vibrations in high-symmetry after experiencing JTE (Supplementary Table 1). For instance, the A2g-symmetric ν23 and B2g-symmetric ν65 in ZnPc would mix with each other, generating two B1g modes (ν023 and ν065) in ZnPc− (Fig. 3a). It should be stressed that the details of this mixing are inaccessible under the excitation of conventional uniform optical fields. As a result, this mixing feature in JTE is completely overlooked in previous studies. A detailed decomposition reveal that the electronic effect leads to redshifts of two modes, resulting in a frequency difference of 4.4 cm−1, as shown in Fig. 3a. It is noted that the displacements of ν23 and ν65 are all located on the lobes with an efficient overlap. Calculated induced dipole moments (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13) determine that the mixing coefficient (see definition in Eq. (1)) between ν23 and ν65 is close to 1.0, which results in distinctly split patterns in ν023 and ν065 as shown in Fig. 3a.

The mixing coefficient could be analogously derived from the perturbational molecular orbital theory as (see a detailed derivation in Supplementary Note 7)

T = λS12 / ΔE

where λ is a fitting parameter, S12 is the overlap between two mixing vibrations, and ΔE is the energy difference. For well-overlapped modes, i.e., S12 close to 1, the mixing coefficient T is inversely proportional to the energy difference ΔE, which is exactly the case of mode mixing for ν23 and ν65. Most of the mixing modes are in this category (Supplementary Figs. 14–16). By collecting all these modes, the fitting parameter λ is determined to be 2.8 cm−1 (see the blue diamond scatters and red line in Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 17).

The theoretical model also predicts another category with S12 = 0, where T becomes zero regardless of ΔE and λ. In fact, there are few modes belonging to this category. For instance, the electronic effect leads to ΔE of 24.3 cm−1 between the A1g-symmetric ν13 and B1g-symmetric ν53 modes. If they were well-overlapped modes, the predicted T would be 0.13. Nevertheless, with no mixing with each other, these two modes give two A1g-symmetric modes in ZnPc−, exhibiting nearly identical fourfold image characteristics to their respective counterparts in ZnPc (Fig. 3c). This result should be attributed to the lack of spatial overlap between ν13 and ν53 modes, which is the sufficient prerequisite of S12 = 0. We note that the frequencies of these two non-overlapping modes change after the JTE, which should be attributed to the symmetry-lowering distortion. Two additional cases fall into this category (see orange diamond scatters in Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 18). We want to stress that the current protocol, i.e., using TERS images to monitor the splitting and determine mixing coefficients of molecular vibrations, can be readily extended to other charge-induced JTE systems (Supplementary Fig. 19) owing to the intrinsic characteristics of nonresonant Raman imaging that can visualize the molecular vibrational modes in real space.36–38

Identifying isotopically engineered JTE distortion
The last capability of TERS imaging proposed in the present work is the identification of the controllable distortion in JTE. To this end, partial isotope substitution is employed to control the direction of JTE distortion, which is experimentally synthesizable47,48 (Supplementary Note 9) and can be selected out via TERS imaging (Supplementary Fig. 20). Although the geometrical variation is as small as 0.010 and 0.026 Å (Fig. 1b), isotope substitutions of 13C and deuterium (D) in one diagonal axis can stabilize the ZnPc−’s elongation configuration along this axis, i.e., iso-1 (Fig. 4a). Calculated results reveal that at the experimental conditions of 7 K and 6 × 10−14 atm, iso-1 has a lower Gibbs free energy of 0.38 kJ mol−1 than the configuration elongated along the other direction (iso-2). The population of iso-1 is then determined to be 99.84% in the experimental conditions (Supplementary Note 10). Because of the almost identical geometries (Fig. 4a), iso-1 and iso-2 are indistinguishable in electronic structure-based SPM techniques even with functionalized tips49–51.

This challenge can be overcome by utilizing the sensitivity of TERS images to subtle variations in vibrational modes (Fig. 4b). Although the calculated TERS image of ν0i1 121a in iso-1 has the identical brightest lobe patterns to that of the counterpart in iso-2, two moderate patterns appear around the interior nitrogen atoms along the isotopic axis for ν0i2 121b in iso-2. Similarly, except for the identical brightest central patterns, moderate patterns arise around the non-isotopic lobes in ν0i1 116a image for iso-1. These results should be attributed to the subtle vibrational redistributions caused by the axial length difference at the sub-ångström level. The ability of TERS imaging to distinguishing such subtle vibrational variations requires highly localized SCP fields (Supplementary Fig. 21), providing an effective means for identifying different configurations arising from isotopic JTE distortion.
paper_content.methods:
Effective field Hamiltonian for TERS
The polarizability of non-resonance Raman under a localized plasmon is evaluated as

ακρσ = ∂α / ∂Qκ |vi⟩ ⟨vf| ...

where ρ and σ represent the Cartesian coordinates, Qκ is vibration modes, |vi⟩ (|vf⟩) is the initial (final) vibrational states of the ground electronic state |Ψg⟩, and

α ρσ = 1/ω ...

with the absorption process operator under Raman scattering

Vbσ = 1/2 Σj (pbj,σgσ + gσpbj,σ) ...

where pbj = i∇j is the momentum operator of the jth electron, and gσ is the amplitude distribution function of localized plasmon in σ direction.

The incident light wavelength was set to 532 nm (2.33 eV), that employed in experiments30 to fulfill the non-resonance condition. The response algorithm was adopted to efficiently evaluate Eq. (3)43, and the central-finite-difference method with 1.0 × 10−3 amu1/2Bohr size was used to estimate the derivative in Eq. (2). For TERS, it is sufficient to evaluate the zz component of Raman polarizability41,52. In practical simulations, the amplitude distribution function gσ for a localized plasmon field was simulated by a s-type Gaussian function as

g = exp(−α(r−rD)2)

where α is exponent, and r represents the coordinate position of plasmon. Here, α can determine the full-width at half-maximum (FWHM), i.e., the size of the localized plasmon field with the relation of FWHM = 2√ln2/√α. Specifically, we set α to be 0.086 Bohr−2 for a 3 Å localized plasmon.

Finally, the intensity of Raman scattering can be calculated by

I = ω4/c4 |MsMd|2 |Fp|2 |ακzz|2

with scattering light frequency of ω, directional radiation factor Md owing to the corresponding nanostructures for the enhancement in the detection direction53, localized plasmon field enhancement factor M, Purcell factor Fp54 that accounts for the spontaneous emission enhancement, and the light speed c. In addition, using Eq. (2), the induced dipole could be calculated by

μ0,k = M Fp αk,0 E0

where E0 is the electric field amplitude of the incident light and the elements of tensor αk,0 are given by Eq. (2). The parameter of μ can represent the signs (positive/negative) of Raman polarizability, that associated with vibration phase55. The Raman polarizability and intensity under localized plasmon field were practically calculated by the FASTERS program56. In addition, all the Raman spectra in the main text were convoluted by a Lorentzian function with FWHM of 10 cm−1.

Computational details
First-principles calculations were based on density functional theory methods, implemented in the GAUSSIAN16 software package, A03 version57. We considered the physisorption of the molecule. In other words, we neglect the substrate, tip, and bias voltage, as shown in TERS setup (Fig. 1a) and the negligible charge transfer from tip. The geometrical structure, electronic structures, and vibrational modes of both neutral ZnPc and anionic ZnPc− molecules were calculated in the gas phase at the B3LYP level58 with the 6-311+G(d,p) basis set59,60, excluding any unphysical convergence of the electronic structures, in particular for anionic states. The effect of anharmonicity on vibrations can be neglected under the cryogenic temperature of 7 K in the TERS experiments (Supplementary Fig. 22)30 because of the rigid structure of ZnPc. In addition, we obtained the electronic effect on the vibrational frequency by computing the neutral-geometry using the vibrational normal modes of the neutral molecule as basis vectors.

Experimental details
All experiment data acquisition were performed in a custom low-temperature and ultrahigh-vacuum scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) (Unisoku 1400) combined with optical detection systems at about 6 K under a base pressure of about 5 × 10−11 Torr. The Ag(100) step substrate was cleaned by several cycles of argon ion sputtering and annealing. Electrochemically etched sliver Ag tips were cleaned by electron-bombardment and argon-ion sputtering. Then, by controlling the tip indentation, an atomistic protrusion was formed as the TERS active tip. The ZnPc molecules were thermally evaporated onto the Ag(100) substrate covered by 3ML-NaCl at 6 K. The supplementary TERS mapping was performed under the following laser conditions: an excitation wavelength of 532 nm and a power of 0.2 mW entering the STM chamber through the glass window. The acquisition parameters were set at V = −1 V and I = 2 pA, with the tip precisely positioned above on the joint position between the molecular lobe and Zn ion. Subsequently, the feedback loop turned off to maintain a constant tip-sample distance. Mapping data were then acquired under these conditions. Each spectrum was acquired for 1 s, resulting in a 60 × 60 pixel image with a total size of 3 nm × 3 nm.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript by Yu, et. al presents a theoretical framework for visualizing the effects related to Jahn-Teller effects in tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy experiments. The authors study how the vibrational modes would change upon charging a molecule. Interestingly, they also observe a spatial localization of the vibrational modes within the molecule, together with vibrational mixing. Lastly, the authors study the effect of isotopes on the vibrational features.
This work is timely, as many groups are pursuing Raman maps of single molecules. Moreover, there is a lot more theory/computational support needed in understanding the experimental results. Given the topic and the nature of the manuscript, I would be glad to recommend this manuscript for Nat. Comms. provided the authors satisfactorily respond to the points below.
In my opinion, there are two voids in this manuscript:
First, the authors do not mention/nor estimate the role of the bias voltages in the Raman maps. While it is true that both neutral and anionic ZnPc can be stable on NaCl (or any other large band gap insulator), for their imaging different voltages need to be applied. Otherwise, the molecule would simply change its charge state. I understand that in some cases there will be a short voltage window at which both could charge states could co-exist, but this will be the minority of the cases.
Second, the authors discuss the spatial localization and splitting of vibrational modes – which I find commendable and very interesting. Yet, the experiments will take place on a surface. Would such effects still be present in asymmetric adsorption positions? How much change would it incur in the vibrational modes? As far as I understand from the ‘Methods’ section, the calculations are done on the gas-phase molecules. Why not take the geometries of the adsorbed molecules?
Here are additional points:
1) In the abstract I would reinforce to the reader about the theoretical nature of this work.
2) Authors claim that the Raman spectra of ZnPc powder is accurately reproduced. Yet, some peaks are not present (around 800 cm-1), while some additional peaks appear (1250 cm-1). It is important to note as to why such discrepancy comes from.
3) Continuing on the text progression: it is unclear as to why the authors compare spectra for ZnPc powder and then proceed to discuss the results of single molecules. I think the flow of the text would be better if this was explicitly linked and motivated in written form.
4) It is unclear as to why the plasmon central position (black cross in Fig 1) is chosen in that particular location. The authors should clarified this in the manuscript.
5) Fig 1c can be difficult to interpreted. I recommend that the authors include colors in the center positions to facilitate comparison.
6) The overlooked vibrational mixing is quite a nice finding. But I think the authors could improve Fig 3, specifically by increasing the size of the arrows in panels a and c. I also do not think it is necessary to show the plot in b from 280 to 300 cm-1, instead more space can be used for panels a and c.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The Jahn-Teller effect (JTE) is a fundamental principle in physics and chemistry, describing how geometric distortion in non-linear molecules lifts electronic degeneracy, thereby playing a crucial role in the properties of molecules and condensed matter systems. This manuscript by Yu et al. presents a theoretical study proposing the use of vibrationally resolved tip-enhanced Raman scattering (TERS) imaging to visualize the vibrational features in a single zinc phthalocyanine (ZnPc) molecule undergoing a charge-induced JTE. The authors report that this approach can image the splitting of degenerate vibrational modes, characterize a previously overlooked mixing of non-degenerate vibrations, and identify JTE distortion configurations engineered by partial isotopic substitution.
However, I cannot recommend this work for publication in Nature Communications in its present form because of the lack of significant conceptual novelty and the discrepancies with existing experimental data. These issues, detailed below, need to be thoroughly addressed.
1) While the proposed application is interesting, the work largely represents an incremental application of an established technique (TERS imaging) to a well-understood phenomenon (JTE). The fact that JTE induces structural distortions and symmetry changes in molecules is a cornerstone of the field, extensively studied by various experimental and theoretical methods. This manuscript proposes a real-space visualization, but the predicted outcomes (e.g., a change from four-fold to two-fold symmetry) are largely intuitive consequences of the effect. The study does not appear to provide a fundamental advance that challenges or significantly expands the conventional understanding of the JTE.
2) The manuscript's central arguments are built upon the accurate assignment of vibrational modes, but the theoretical results show evident deviations from the cited experimental data (Ref. 16). For instance, in Figure 1c, the calculated frequency for the mode near 1486 cm−1 in neutral and charged ZnPc molecules does not align well with the experimentally measured peaks. More critically, the experimentally observed blueshift for this mode upon charging the molecule is much smaller than the shift predicted by the authors' calculations (Fig. 1c). This discrepancy casts considerable doubt on the reliability of the theoretical model. More robust analysis for the peak assignments is required.
3) The ability to resolve the image differences in the TERS images shown in Figure 4 is highly dependent on the spatial confinement of the plasmonic field. The authors should discuss the influence of the plasmonic field's confinement on the identification of the JTE. Specifically, what level of spatial resolution is necessary to distinguish the subtle vibrational changes predicted in the manuscript?
4) The study does not address the synthetic feasibility of the proposed isotopically substituted molecule. Proposing a theoretical case is useful only if it is experimentally realizable. The authors should consider to propose plans that are more readily verifiable in experiments to strengthen the link between their theory and practical application.
5) Minor point: The section title "Controlling JTE distortion by partial isotope substitution" seems misleading. The section does not propose a method to control the distortion but rather to identify a pre-determined distortion in a chemically synthesized molecule. The section title should be changed.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This paper introduces a TERS imaging protocol that visualizes how individual vibrational modes evolve as a single ZnPc molecule undergoes charge-induced Jahn-Teller distortion. The authors accurately reproduce normal Raman and previously reported TESR spectra for both neutral and anionic ZnPc, validating their plasmon-embedded field Hamiltonian approach. Although the JTE arises from vibronic coupling, previous works have mostly imaged symmetry-broken electronic orbitals; examining only the electronic component of the JTE thus limits these studies to partial observation. Direct imaging of the vibrational component is therefore crucial for enhancing the predictive accuracy of structure-property models, and the authors’ attempt to resolve and independently image the vibrational modes is both timely and valuable. However, the following points require further explanation.
1. All Raman images in this paper are theoretical. The experimental data is only the 1D Raman spectrum, while the Raman images are entirely simulations created by virtually scanning the plasmon local field and calculating the polarizability and enhancement factor for each mode. Even at very low resolution, experimental data is needed to validate the theoretical Raman imaging.
2. The calculation model assumes a 3Å Gaussian plasmon and fixed orientation. Sensitivity to apex shape, gap size and charge-transfer strength should be quantified to solve tip-apex dependence.
3. When discussing symmetry splittings such as those arising from JTE, the relative frequency shifts are paramount, and temperature-induced offsets largely cancel out. Nonetheless, vibrational modes obtained under the idealized assumptions of 0 K and the harmonic approximation can diverge from those observed in real experimental environments. The manuscript should therefore include further clarification on how temperature and anharmonicity corrections were applied.
4. The protocol is demonstrated for only one molecule (ZnPc). Establishing its universality would ideally involve applying the workflow to at least one additional system. Given that suh simulations may be computationally demanding, the authors could instead strengthen the manuscript by adding a discussion of how the approach could be extended to other molecular system and what challenges might be encountered.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
In this manuscript, the authors propose to use imaging based on tip-enhanced Raman scattering as a means of accessing vibrational states in molecules that undergo Kahn-Teller distortions. For that, they build computational methods to obtain effective Hamiltonian models for Raman polarizability and scattering cross sections taking into account vibrational states defined according to relevant irreducible representations for the pertinent point group symmetries. In the model, they use localized plasmon fields represented by Gaussian functions. Additional first-principles calculations based on DFT to obtain electronic structures and vibrational modes of the the ZnPc molecule. The outcomes of the computational modeling are compared with experimental data supported from external references.
Through theoretical insights, the authors propose that imaging with Raman techniques allows to identify specific vibrational modes and their spatial distribution, which becomes all-important when aiming at gathering information when molecules are subject to Jahn-Teller distortions. In particular, the authors can describe through their model the observed frequency shifts when the charge state of molecules is changed by electrical biases, inducing Jahn-Teller effects after the charge injection. They explore how the modes change upon symmetry lowering and explain why some of the modes resulting from the JT-induced splitting are observed in experiments and why others are not. Additionally, they propose that TERS experiments can be aimed at exploring mixing of vibrational modes that is forbidden for high-symmetry settings, but can become mixed when symmetry is lowered by JT effects. Lastly, they also show how TERS imaging could be used to probe changes in vibrational modes caused by isotopic substitutions.
The work is relevant because most of works have focused on the effects of JT on the electronic component, rather than the vibrational ones resulting from JT vibronic couplings. I believe that this is an interesting perspective for experimentalists to explore what Raman-based imaging can gather about vibronic states in molecules. Therefore, I judge this is work is relevant to the field.
I have some comments:
When referring to Ref. 16, the authors assume an interpretation of the spectral variations in ZnPc as charges are injected as arising from JT effects. However, if I am not wrong, the authors do not interpret directly such variations as resulting from JT effects. The sentence as it is written, presumes that the authors of that paper assume JT effects as the reason of the observed changes in spectra.
In Fig. 1 c, the blue shift of the resonance at 1486 cm-1 between neutral ZnPc and ZnPc- is very subtle. I recommend to make the shift more evident in the figure (e.g., adding a vertical dashed line).
For a more accessible reading, I recommend to add a schematic illustration in the main text of all the irreps and corresponding point-group symmetries (before and after JT) for the relevant modes in the spectral range covered by Fig. 1. When reading the paper, it was difficult to me to finally grasp the irreps of the modes discussed in that figure.

Point-by-point response to the Referee #2’s comments:
General Comment: The Jahn-Teller effect (JTE) is a fundamental principle in physics
and chemistry, describing how geometric distortion in non-linear molecules lifts
electronic degeneracy, thereby playing a crucial role in the properties of molecules and
condensed matter systems. This manuscript by Yu et al. presents a theoretical study
proposing the use of vibrationally resolved tip-enhanced Raman scattering (TERS)
imaging to visualize the vibrational features in a single zinc phthalocyanine (ZnPc)
molecule undergoing a charge-induced JTE. The authors report that this approach can
image the splitting of degenerate vibrational modes, characterize a previously
overlooked mixing of non-degenerate vibrations, and identify JTE distortion
configurations engineered by partial isotopic substitution.
However, I cannot recommend this work for publication in Nature Communications in
its present form because of the lack of significant conceptual novelty and the
discrepancies with existing experimental data. These issues, detailed below, need to be
thoroughly addressed.
Reply: We thank the Referee for giving us an opportunity to highlight the novelty and
clarify the differences between theoretical and experimental results. As noted by the
Referee, the Jahn-Teller effect (JTE) utilizes vibronic coupling to lift electronic
degeneracy of non-linear molecules. By definition, the vibrational aspect is equally
important as the electronic component in JTE. Nevertheless, owing to the lack of
appropriate tools, only the electronic component of JTE is extensively investigated in
the literature. In this work, we propose that by leveraging spatially confined plasmons,
high-resolution TERS imaging is an ideal means to visualize the vibrational evolution
when a molecule undergoes JTE. In this scenario, the spectral outcomes are totally
different from those excited by uniform fields (see following R1 for details). In other
words, we provide a novel approach for high-resolution probing of the vibrational
aspect in JTE, which comprehensively deepens its fundamental understanding.
After careful and comprehensive comparison, we find that, as pointed out by the
Referee, there is indeed a difference for one peak between the theoretically predicted
spectra and the experimental measurements. Otherwise, the calculated spectra are in
overall agreement with the experimental data. To achieve a definitive assignment of the
only questionable peak, we seek assistance from our experimental collaborators. The
newly updated experimental Raman imaging of this peak shows excellent agreement
with the theoretical prediction, confirming the consistency between our calculations
and the experimental data (see following R2 for details).
Overall, with the help of the Referee, we have highlighted the conceptual novelty and
eliminated the potential discrepancy with the experimental data. These improvements
have significantly enhanced the robustness and reliability of the present work. We hope
that the current revision meets the publication criteria of Nature Communications.
Following is a point-by-point response to the Referee’s detailed comments.
Q1: While the proposed application is interesting, the work largely represents an
incremental application of an established technique (TERS imaging) to a well-
understood phenomenon (JTE). The fact that JTE induces structural distortions and
symmetry changes in molecules is a cornerstone of the field, extensively studied by
various experimental and theoretical methods. This manuscript proposes a real-space
visualization, but the predicted outcomes (e.g., a change from four-fold to two-fold
symmetry) are largely intuitive consequences of the effect. The study does not appear
to provide a fundamental advance that challenges or significantly expands the
conventional understanding of the JTE.
R1: We thank the Referee for allowing us to highlight the novelty of our work in a
revision. We agree with the Referee that in the present work, an advanced vibrationally
resolved technique, i.e., high-resolution TERS imaging, is used to investigate the JTE
that involves vibronic coupling. While the electronic structure changes associated with
JTE distortion have been extensively studied both theoretically and experimentally, the
equally important vibrational aspect has not yet been investigated with high spatial
resolution. To this end, high-resolution TERS imaging is a candidate, in which the
spatially confined plasmon (SCP) is a prerequisite. In this context, the spectral
outcomes of JTE are quite different from those under uniform optical fields. As pointed
out by the Referee, the latter, in particular, the frequency splitting of the degenerate
vibrations, is well known. Specially:
1) As a consequence of structural distortions induced by JTE, a degenerate mode (E
u
modes in the present work) should split into two modes. Intuitively, we can expect that
one corresponding Raman band splits into two Raman bands. This is true under uniform
optical fields. Nevertheless, accompanied by the splitting, a localization of the
corresponding vibrational mode occurs. Because SCP can only shine on a part of the
molecule, in this context, the spectral outcome of JTE only results in one band when
the SCP is located at one specific position (see Fig. 2b in the main text for details). On
the other hand, the localization of the split modes can be visualized by TERS imaging
(see Fig. 2c in the main text for details), which is inaccessible under the conventional
uniform optical fields. In other words, our work expands the understanding even for the
well-studied frequency splitting in JTE.
2) Fundamental group theory tells us that symmetry reduction can cause different
irreducible representations under high symmetry to become the same irreducible
representation under low symmetry, i.e., vibrational modes mixing after JTE-induced
distortions. However, group theory only tells us that the mixing exists, but not how it
occurs in detail. Again, conventional uniform optical fields cannot investigate the
details of this mixing. As a result, this feature in JTE is overlooked in previous studies.
In the present work, we reveal that TERS imaging is a perfect means for studying the
mode mixing in JTE. Not only modes’ evolution but also mixing coefficients can be
precisely determined by TERS imaging, providing a fundamental understanding of the
JTE.
3) Typically, the distortions induced by JTE are unbiased. Although partial isotopic
substitution could, in principle, modulate JTE distortions, precisely distinguishing these
structural variations is a challenge. In the present work, we demonstrate that because of
its sensitivity to subtle variations in vibrational modes, TERS imaging can effectively
identify isomers with different isotopic substitutions. This finding paves the way for
further applications of the vibrational aspect in JTE.
Overall, this work focuses on the visualization of the vibrational aspect in JTE, a highly
important yet difficult-to-investigate subject due to the lack of appropriate tools. We
demonstrate that high-resolution TERS imaging is an emerging tool for this purpose,
where the spectral outcomes are totally different from those under uniform fields. The
findings in the present work not only provide a deep and fundamental understanding of
the JTE effect but also pave the way for its further practical applications. Therefore, we
believe that our work represents a substantial advance rather than an incremental
contribution to JTE.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In the response, the authors have largely replied to my comments. You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The Jahn-Teller effect (JTE) reduces the geometrical symmetry of a system with degenerate electronic states via vibronic coupling, playing a pivotal role in molecular and condensed systems. However, due to the intrinsic limitations of conventional techniques, only the electronic evolution in JTE can be measured. Herein, we theoretically propose that vibrational resolved tip-enhanced Raman scattering images can visualize the vibrational evolutions in JTE in real space. Taking an experimentally accessible single zinc phthalocyanine (ZnPc) molecule as a proof-of-principle example, not only the degenerate vibrational splitting but also the overlooked vibration mixing caused by the JTE in its anionic form can be characterized by Raman images. Leveraging Raman images, the controllable configuration of JTE distortion with partial isotopic substitution can be further identified. These findings establish a practical protocol to monitor the detailed vibrational evolutions when a single molecule experiences JTE, providing a pathway for visualization of spontaneous symmetry breaking in molecular and solid-state systems.

---

## Introduction

The Jahn-Teller effect (JTE)1,2 describes a fundamental phenomenon that a degenerate system spontaneously reduces its geometry symmetry via the vibronic coupling to stabilize the total energy3–5. JTE represents a general mechanism of spontaneous symmetry breaking, which is responsible for various important observations across multiple disciplines, including spectroscopy, molecular and solid-state physics, stereochemistry, and materials science6–14. In practice, JTE can be efficiently induced by injecting or removing an electron from a degenerate electronic state15,16, particularly in systems containing transition metal ions7,17,18. Such a charge-induced JTE arises from the modification of electronic occupancy, which directly lifts the degeneracy of molecular orbitals and thereby triggers symmetry-lowering structural distortions. In this context, scanning probe microscopy (SPM) techniques provide a practical means to precisely control JTE in real space19,20.

Despite the success of SPM techniques in the visualization of JTE, most investigations were focused on imaging the symmetry breaking of electronic states21–25. Exclusive investigation on the electronic degrees of freedom in JTE has led to the current lack of understanding of its vibrational aspect, which results in potentially ambiguous assignments of accompanying frequency splitting, the mixing of vibrational wavefunctions upon symmetry reduction, and the possibility of controlling JTE distortions through atomic displacements. Recently, by leveraging the tip-enhanced Raman scatting (TERS)26–29, an experimental measurement has captured several spectral variations when a single zinc phthalocyanine (ZnPc) was negatively charged30, where vibrational frequency evolution was highlighted. Nevertheless, it still lacks further reports on imaging vibrational symmetry breaking, another essential aspect of JTE, although it is possible owing to the high spatial resolution of TERS31–35.

Recent TERS studies have demonstrated their ability to quantitatively map the spatial distribution of vibrational wavefunctions32,36–39. In this study, this technique is expected to be further extended to visualize the single-molecule JTE from the vibrational perspective. Taking the experimentally accessible ZnPc molecule as a proof-of-principle example, we theoretically propose that TERS images provide a practical means to monitor all the details of the vibrational evolution in JTE distortion. We demonstrate that, not only the splitting of degenerate vibrations but also the mixing of non-degenerate vibrations belonging to different irreducible representations of the high-symmetry point group, can be affirmatively observed in TERS images. For the latter case, we reveal that the mixing strength is determined by both the energy difference and spatial distribution overlap between the mixed modes. Moreover, we manifest that the controllable JTE distortions at the sub-ångström level achieved through partial isotope substitution can be unambiguously distinguished by high-resolution TERS imaging.

---

## Results

Spectra characterization of charge-induced JTE
Figure 1a illustrates the experimental setup for injecting an electron into neutral ZnPc to induce JTE distortion. In the neutral state, ZnPc possesses a doubly degenerate lowest unoccupied molecular orbital. Upon adding an extra electron, this degeneracy is lifted, triggering a symmetry-lowering structural distortion. Previous experiments observed sudden changes in TERS spectra when the sample bias exceeded 0.3 V, which was assigned as a transition from the neutral to negatively charged state30. It should be stressed that owing to the insulating spacer layer introduced in Fig. 1a, the negatively charged ZnPc− has a sufficiently long lifetime for spectral measurements and even imaging30,40. Besides, the experiment explicitly ruled out molecular deformation induced by mechanical pressure from the tip apex. Specifically, the reproducible spectral evolution during tip approach and retraction confirmed that the observed spectral changes and symmetry reduction originated intrinsically from different charging states of ZnPc30. Calculations show that the JTE-induced geometrical distortion from the neutral D4h to the anionic D2h is quite subtle (the elongations along both the diagonal axes are 0.026 and 0.010 Å, respectively, as shown in Fig. 1b), which provides an ideal example for focusing exclusively on vibrational variation itself.

To efficiently excite the required highly localized plasmonic field for single-molecule TERS measurements, an incident light with a wavelength of 532 nm was employed in the experiments30. Under the same incident energy, our first-principles calculations accurately reproduce the corresponding observed Raman spectra of ZnPc powder30 except for few peaks with relative intensities below ≈5% of the strongest band (e.g., a peak around 800 cm−1, Fig. 1c). Theoretical analysis reveal that these peaks originate from Raman-inactive modes because of the symmetry breaking via molecular stacking and lattice interactions in ZnPc powder. This undesired symmetry breaking is absent for a single molecule. Thus, the experimentally adopted wavelength of 532 nm can be used without further calibration in the practical calculations for single-molecular TERS. Then, we adopt an effective field Hamiltonian approach (see “Methods” for details), in which the spatial amplitude distribution of the localized plasmonic field is incorporated as the quantized light-matter interaction operator33,41–44, to enable the quantitative simulation of bond-resolved TERS spectra. By placing a 3 Å spatially confined plasmon (SCP) at the same tip position in the experiments, i.e., above the joint position between the lobe and center of ZnPc (see the black cross in Fig. 1b), the calculated TERS spectra for both neutral ZnPc and anionic ZnPc− are in overall agreement with their experimental counterparts (Fig. 1d). Specifically, the two main bands in the calculated spectrum of ZnPc− are located at 1309 and 1512 cm−1, which are in good agreement with the experimental values of 1305 and 1518 cm−1. For neutral ZnPc, one main peak in the theoretical spectrum appears at 1348 cm−1, which is again in agreement with the experimentally measured band at 1340 cm−1. As a result, the calculated TERS spectrum of ZnPc− presents a 39 cm−1 redshift caused by JTE, which quantitatively agrees with the corresponding experimental observation of 35 cm−1.30 For another main band, although the frequency shifts are in qualitative agreement, the theoretically predicted blueshift (26 cm−1) is larger than that (7 cm−1) measured in the experiments30. This result arises from the sole frequency deviation of the peak for neutral ZnPc, i.e., the band around 1511 cm−1 observed in experiments, as shown in Fig. 1d. Further calculated and experimental Raman images (see “Methods” for details) for this band are in excellent agreement with each other (Supplementary Fig. 1), demonstrating the affirmative assignment of this main band. In addition, the JTE-induced shifts of other secondary bands in the calculated spectra also agree well with the experimentally observed redshifts (Supplementary Fig. 2). The reproduction of the measured references in both uniform and plasmonic fields validates the accurate descriptions of electronic and vibrational structures as well as their responses at the current theoretical level.

According to the calculations, the experimentally measured30 two dominant bands for ZnPc and ZnPc− (Fig. 1d) are assigned to different vibrational modes. Specifically, the degenerate ν108 and ν105 contribute to the dominant bands of ZnPc. In ZnPc−, these vibrations split as a consequence of JTE and are labeled with subscripts “a” and “b” hereafter. As a result, the dominant high-frequency band originates from the accidentally degenerate ν0103a and ν025, where the superscript “0” denotes the anionic form. Meanwhile, ν048 contributes to the dominant band with low frequency, with the shoulder assigned as ν0108b. Although this assignment is different from ref. 30, the observation of only a single splitting component, i.e., ν0108b in ZnPc−, indicates the spatial localization of degenerate vibrational modes during symmetry breaking induced by JTE.

Imaging the degenerate vibrational splitting
To directly visualize the localization, we turn to vibrationally resolved TERS imaging36–38,45,46. By moving tip positions and simultaneously collecting scattering intensities at a given Raman shift, the images of the two dominant bands of ZnPc under an experimentally feasible 3 Å SCP (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4)37 were calculated as shown in Fig. 2a. Both images exhibit clear fourfold symmetrical patterns, which correspond to the Eu irreducible representation in D4h point group (see vibrational displacements in Fig. 2a). On the other hand, the dominant modes of ZnPc− give two-fold symmetric patterns (Fig. 2a), demonstrating the symmetry reduction from D4h to D2h owing to JTE. The individual contributions of component modes to images in Fig. 2a can be found in Supplementary Figs. 5–7. It should be stressed that, although bias voltages and a decoupled substrate were used to stabilized different charge states of ZnPc30, these effects on the vibrational modes and Raman images are negligible (Supplementary Figs. 8–10). This result is consistent with the general purpose of introducing the decouple layer in TERS experiments30 and should be attributed to the rigid backbone and flat adsorption configuration of ZnPc. For other systems with strong substrate-adsorbate interactions, adequately large cluster models with advanced charge localization calculations would be required for the accurate description of the substrate effects.

Detailed analysis reveal that at the central Zn position, the image of ν048 is constructive, which is opposite to the destructive feature in that of ν108. This result further confirms that the dominant bands observed in experiments30 originate from different vibrational modes. To determine the split modes of degenerate vibrations, for example, ν108 that involves vibrations at four interior nitrogen atoms, we focused a 3 Å SCP on the nitrogen atoms along different axes in ZnPc− (see the color-marked crosses in the inset of Fig. 2b). The calculated spectra manifest that when the SCP is located at one specific position, one split mode becomes active and another one is completely suppressed (Fig. 2b), which arises from the vibrational localization accompanying with the splitting of degenerate modes. These spectral outcomes of JTE under plasmonic fields are quite different from those under conventional uniform optical fields, where both split Raman bands can be simultaneously observed in the latter. As a result, the split modes (ν0108a and ν0108b) can be identified. Specifically, TERS images of these vibrations exhibit split patterns derived from the original ν108, with a destructive center, as anticipated (Fig. 2c).

With the correct assignment, the electronic and displacement redistribution effects can be unambiguously investigated for the splitting of degenerate vibrations when the molecule experiences a JTE distortion. Particularly, adding an extra electron to neutral D4h ZnPc would split the degenerate ν108 at 1348.0 cm−1 into a blue-shifted mode at 1352.5 cm−1 and a significantly red-shifted mode at 1319.6 cm−1. The Eu ν108 mode then becomes further localized, which results in two non-degenerate modes, i.e., a B2u mode (ν0108a) at 1345.6 cm−1 and a B3u mode (ν0108b) at 1323.5 cm−1 (Fig. 2c). The decomposition of electronic and vibrational effects is a general approach. The detailed analysis for other representative degenerate modes can be found in Supplementary Fig. 11. It should be stressed that the minor geometrical distortion caused by JTE in ZnPc enables the decomposition of these effects.

Imaging the non-degenerate vibrational mixing
The minor geometrical distortion also allows explicit visualization of another vibrational evolution, i.e., the mixing of non-degenerate vibrations in high-symmetry after experiencing JTE (Supplementary Table 1). For instance, the A2g-symmetric ν23 and B2g-symmetric ν65 in ZnPc would mix with each other, generating two B1g modes (ν023 and ν065) in ZnPc− (Fig. 3a). It should be stressed that the details of this mixing are inaccessible under the excitation of conventional uniform optical fields. As a result, this mixing feature in JTE is completely overlooked in previous studies. A detailed decomposition reveal that the electronic effect leads to redshifts of two modes, resulting in a frequency difference of 4.4 cm−1, as shown in Fig. 3a. It is noted that the displacements of ν23 and ν65 are all located on the lobes with an efficient overlap. Calculated induced dipole moments (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13) determine that the mixing coefficient (see definition in Eq. (1)) between ν23 and ν65 is close to 1.0, which results in distinctly split patterns in ν023 and ν065 as shown in Fig. 3a.

The mixing coefficient could be analogously derived from the perturbational molecular orbital theory as (see a detailed derivation in Supplementary Note 7)

T = λS12 / ΔE

where λ is a fitting parameter, S12 is the overlap between two mixing vibrations, and ΔE is the energy difference. For well-overlapped modes, i.e., S12 close to 1, the mixing coefficient T is inversely proportional to the energy difference ΔE, which is exactly the case of mode mixing for ν23 and ν65. Most of the mixing modes are in this category (Supplementary Figs. 14–16). By collecting all these modes, the fitting parameter λ is determined to be 2.8 cm−1 (see the blue diamond scatters and red line in Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 17).

The theoretical model also predicts another category with S12 = 0, where T becomes zero regardless of ΔE and λ. In fact, there are few modes belonging to this category. For instance, the electronic effect leads to ΔE of 24.3 cm−1 between the A1g-symmetric ν13 and B1g-symmetric ν53 modes. If they were well-overlapped modes, the predicted T would be 0.13. Nevertheless, with no mixing with each other, these two modes give two A1g-symmetric modes in ZnPc−, exhibiting nearly identical fourfold image characteristics to their respective counterparts in ZnPc (Fig. 3c). This result should be attributed to the lack of spatial overlap between ν13 and ν53 modes, which is the sufficient prerequisite of S12 = 0. We note that the frequencies of these two non-overlapping modes change after the JTE, which should be attributed to the symmetry-lowering distortion. Two additional cases fall into this category (see orange diamond scatters in Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 18). We want to stress that the current protocol, i.e., using TERS images to monitor the splitting and determine mixing coefficients of molecular vibrations, can be readily extended to other charge-induced JTE systems (Supplementary Fig. 19) owing to the intrinsic characteristics of nonresonant Raman imaging that can visualize the molecular vibrational modes in real space.36–38

Identifying isotopically engineered JTE distortion
The last capability of TERS imaging proposed in the present work is the identification of the controllable distortion in JTE. To this end, partial isotope substitution is employed to control the direction of JTE distortion, which is experimentally synthesizable47,48 (Supplementary Note 9) and can be selected out via TERS imaging (Supplementary Fig. 20). Although the geometrical variation is as small as 0.010 and 0.026 Å (Fig. 1b), isotope substitutions of 13C and deuterium (D) in one diagonal axis can stabilize the ZnPc−’s elongation configuration along this axis, i.e., iso-1 (Fig. 4a). Calculated results reveal that at the experimental conditions of 7 K and 6 × 10−14 atm, iso-1 has a lower Gibbs free energy of 0.38 kJ mol−1 than the configuration elongated along the other direction (iso-2). The population of iso-1 is then determined to be 99.84% in the experimental conditions (Supplementary Note 10). Because of the almost identical geometries (Fig. 4a), iso-1 and iso-2 are indistinguishable in electronic structure-based SPM techniques even with functionalized tips49–51.

This challenge can be overcome by utilizing the sensitivity of TERS images to subtle variations in vibrational modes (Fig. 4b). Although the calculated TERS image of ν0i1 121a in iso-1 has the identical brightest lobe patterns to that of the counterpart in iso-2, two moderate patterns appear around the interior nitrogen atoms along the isotopic axis for ν0i2 121b in iso-2. Similarly, except for the identical brightest central patterns, moderate patterns arise around the non-isotopic lobes in ν0i1 116a image for iso-1. These results should be attributed to the subtle vibrational redistributions caused by the axial length difference at the sub-ångström level. The ability of TERS imaging to distinguishing such subtle vibrational variations requires highly localized SCP fields (Supplementary Fig. 21), providing an effective means for identifying different configurations arising from isotopic JTE distortion.

---

## Methods

Effective field Hamiltonian for TERS
The polarizability of non-resonance Raman under a localized plasmon is evaluated as

ακρσ = ∂α / ∂Qκ |vi⟩ ⟨vf| ...

where ρ and σ represent the Cartesian coordinates, Qκ is vibration modes, |vi⟩ (|vf⟩) is the initial (final) vibrational states of the ground electronic state |Ψg⟩, and

α ρσ = 1/ω ...

with the absorption process operator under Raman scattering

Vbσ = 1/2 Σj (pbj,σgσ + gσpbj,σ) ...

where pbj = i∇j is the momentum operator of the jth electron, and gσ is the amplitude distribution function of localized plasmon in σ direction.

The incident light wavelength was set to 532 nm (2.33 eV), that employed in experiments30 to fulfill the non-resonance condition. The response algorithm was adopted to efficiently evaluate Eq. (3)43, and the central-finite-difference method with 1.0 × 10−3 amu1/2Bohr size was used to estimate the derivative in Eq. (2). For TERS, it is sufficient to evaluate the zz component of Raman polarizability41,52. In practical simulations, the amplitude distribution function gσ for a localized plasmon field was simulated by a s-type Gaussian function as

g = exp(−α(r−rD)2)

where α is exponent, and r represents the coordinate position of plasmon. Here, α can determine the full-width at half-maximum (FWHM), i.e., the size of the localized plasmon field with the relation of FWHM = 2√ln2/√α. Specifically, we set α to be 0.086 Bohr−2 for a 3 Å localized plasmon.

Finally, the intensity of Raman scattering can be calculated by

I = ω4/c4 |MsMd|2 |Fp|2 |ακzz|2

with scattering light frequency of ω, directional radiation factor Md owing to the corresponding nanostructures for the enhancement in the detection direction53, localized plasmon field enhancement factor M, Purcell factor Fp54 that accounts for the spontaneous emission enhancement, and the light speed c. In addition, using Eq. (2), the induced dipole could be calculated by

μ0,k = M Fp αk,0 E0

where E0 is the electric field amplitude of the incident light and the elements of tensor αk,0 are given by Eq. (2). The parameter of μ can represent the signs (positive/negative) of Raman polarizability, that associated with vibration phase55. The Raman polarizability and intensity under localized plasmon field were practically calculated by the FASTERS program56. In addition, all the Raman spectra in the main text were convoluted by a Lorentzian function with FWHM of 10 cm−1.

Computational details
First-principles calculations were based on density functional theory methods, implemented in the GAUSSIAN16 software package, A03 version57. We considered the physisorption of the molecule. In other words, we neglect the substrate, tip, and bias voltage, as shown in TERS setup (Fig. 1a) and the negligible charge transfer from tip. The geometrical structure, electronic structures, and vibrational modes of both neutral ZnPc and anionic ZnPc− molecules were calculated in the gas phase at the B3LYP level58 with the 6-311+G(d,p) basis set59,60, excluding any unphysical convergence of the electronic structures, in particular for anionic states. The effect of anharmonicity on vibrations can be neglected under the cryogenic temperature of 7 K in the TERS experiments (Supplementary Fig. 22)30 because of the rigid structure of ZnPc. In addition, we obtained the electronic effect on the vibrational frequency by computing the neutral-geometry using the vibrational normal modes of the neutral molecule as basis vectors.

Experimental details
All experiment data acquisition were performed in a custom low-temperature and ultrahigh-vacuum scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) (Unisoku 1400) combined with optical detection systems at about 6 K under a base pressure of about 5 × 10−11 Torr. The Ag(100) step substrate was cleaned by several cycles of argon ion sputtering and annealing. Electrochemically etched sliver Ag tips were cleaned by electron-bombardment and argon-ion sputtering. Then, by controlling the tip indentation, an atomistic protrusion was formed as the TERS active tip. The ZnPc molecules were thermally evaporated onto the Ag(100) substrate covered by 3ML-NaCl at 6 K. The supplementary TERS mapping was performed under the following laser conditions: an excitation wavelength of 532 nm and a power of 0.2 mW entering the STM chamber through the glass window. The acquisition parameters were set at V = −1 V and I = 2 pA, with the tip precisely positioned above on the joint position between the molecular lobe and Zn ion. Subsequently, the feedback loop turned off to maintain a constant tip-sample distance. Mapping data were then acquired under these conditions. Each spectrum was acquired for 1 s, resulting in a 60 × 60 pixel image with a total size of 3 nm × 3 nm.

### Reviewer 2

The Jahn-Teller effect (JTE) is a fundamental principle in physics and chemistry, describing how geometric distortion in non-linear molecules lifts electronic degeneracy, thereby playing a crucial role in the properties of molecules and condensed matter systems. This manuscript by Yu et al. presents a theoretical study proposing the use of vibrationally resolved tip-enhanced Raman scattering (TERS) imaging to visualize the vibrational features in a single zinc phthalocyanine (ZnPc) molecule undergoing a charge-induced JTE. The authors report that this approach can image the splitting of degenerate vibrational modes, characterize a previously overlooked mixing of non-degenerate vibrations, and identify JTE distortion configurations engineered by partial isotopic substitution.
However, I cannot recommend this work for publication in Nature Communications in its present form because of the lack of significant conceptual novelty and the discrepancies with existing experimental data. These issues, detailed below, need to be thoroughly addressed.
1) While the proposed application is interesting, the work largely represents an incremental application of an established technique (TERS imaging) to a well-understood phenomenon (JTE). The fact that JTE induces structural distortions and symmetry changes in molecules is a cornerstone of the field, extensively studied by various experimental and theoretical methods. This manuscript proposes a real-space visualization, but the predicted outcomes (e.g., a change from four-fold to two-fold symmetry) are largely intuitive consequences of the effect. The study does not appear to provide a fundamental advance that challenges or significantly expands the conventional understanding of the JTE.
2) The manuscript's central arguments are built upon the accurate assignment of vibrational modes, but the theoretical results show evident deviations from the cited experimental data (Ref. 16). For instance, in Figure 1c, the calculated frequency for the mode near 1486 cm−1 in neutral and charged ZnPc molecules does not align well with the experimentally measured peaks. More critically, the experimentally observed blueshift for this mode upon charging the molecule is much smaller than the shift predicted by the authors' calculations (Fig. 1c). This discrepancy casts considerable doubt on the reliability of the theoretical model. More robust analysis for the peak assignments is required.
3) The ability to resolve the image differences in the TERS images shown in Figure 4 is highly dependent on the spatial confinement of the plasmonic field. The authors should discuss the influence of the plasmonic field's confinement on the identification of the JTE. Specifically, what level of spatial resolution is necessary to distinguish the subtle vibrational changes predicted in the manuscript?
4) The study does not address the synthetic feasibility of the proposed isotopically substituted molecule. Proposing a theoretical case is useful only if it is experimentally realizable. The authors should consider to propose plans that are more readily verifiable in experiments to strengthen the link between their theory and practical application.
5) Minor point: The section title "Controlling JTE distortion by partial isotope substitution" seems misleading. The section does not propose a method to control the distortion but rather to identify a pre-determined distortion in a chemically synthesized molecule. The section title should be changed.

This paper introduces a TERS imaging protocol that visualizes how individual vibrational modes evolve as a single ZnPc molecule undergoes charge-induced Jahn-Teller distortion. ## Paper

## Abstract

The Jahn-Teller effect (JTE) reduces the geometrical symmetry of a system with degenerate electronic states via vibronic coupling, playing a pivotal role in molecular and condensed systems. However, due to the intrinsic limitations of conventional techniques, only the electronic evolution in JTE can be measured. Herein, we theoretically propose that vibrational resolved tip-enhanced Raman scattering images can visualize the vibrational evolutions in JTE in real space. Taking an experimentally accessible single zinc phthalocyanine (ZnPc) molecule as a proof-of-principle example, not only the degenerate vibrational splitting but also the overlooked vibration mixing caused by the JTE in its anionic form can be characterized by Raman images. Leveraging Raman images, the controllable configuration of JTE distortion with partial isotopic substitution can be further identified. These findings establish a practical protocol to monitor the detailed vibrational evolutions when a single molecule experiences JTE, providing a pathway for visualization of spontaneous symmetry breaking in molecular and solid-state systems.
